title: Scoped services in middleware (constructor vs InvokeAsync)
hook: Injecting a scoped DbContext into middleware constructor creates a captive dependency — one context for the app lifetime. Resolve scoped services in InvokeAsync or use IMiddleware instead.

blocks.text: Dependency injection (DI) in ASP.NET Core registers services as singleton, scoped, or transient. Middleware classes built with UseMiddleware<T> are constructed once at startup as singletons. If you inject a scoped service like DbContext or a per-request tenant service into the constructor, the container may allow it at startup but you get one instance captured forever — the captive dependency anti-pattern. Correct approach: inject scoped services as InvokeAsync method parameters, use IMiddleware with IMiddlewareFactory, or resolve from HttpContext.RequestServices inside InvokeAsync.

entries.plainDefinition: One instance per HTTP request within the request scope.
A longer-lived object holds a reference to a shorter-lived service, extending its lifetime incorrectly.
entries.example: Singleton middleware ctor injecting scoped DbContext

entries.plainDefinition: Creates IMiddleware instances per request with correct scoped resolution.
entries.example: Built-in when using app.UseMiddleware<MyMiddleware>() with IMiddleware

entries.plainDefinition: Per-request IServiceProvider for resolving scoped and transient services.

blocks.text: Captive DbContext in middleware causes stale data, thread-safety violations, and memory leaks — Entity Framework Core contexts are not thread-safe and must not outlive the request. Reddit r/dotnet and LeetCode discuss this as a top ASP.NET Core interview question alongside middleware order. Production symptoms: random wrong tenant data, ObjectDisposedException under load, or growing memory from never-disposed contexts.

blocks.title: The rule
blocks.body: Singleton middleware constructor: only singleton dependencies. Scoped dependencies: InvokeAsync parameters, IMiddleware, or RequestServices inside InvokeAsync.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Request scope created
items.body: Host creates a scope at the start of each HTTP request.

items.title: Middleware InvokeAsync called
items.body: Framework resolves method-injected scoped services from the request scope.

items.title: Service used for one request
items.body: DbContext tracks entities only for this request.

items.title: Scope disposed
items.body: End of request disposes scoped services including DbContext.

diagram.title: Captive dependency vs InvokeAsync injection
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  subgraph wrong["WRONG — constructor injection"]
    SM[Singleton Middleware] -->|holds forever| SC[Scoped DbContext]
  end
  subgraph right["CORRECT — InvokeAsync injection"]
    REQ[Request Scope] --> MW[Middleware InvokeAsync]
    REQ --> DB[Scoped DbContext]
    MW --> DB
    REQ -->|dispose end request| X[Disposed]
  end

snippet.label: WRONG — scoped DbContext in constructor
snippet.explanation: DbContext injected at startup lives for the application lifetime. Concurrent requests share one context — undefined behavior and exceptions.

snippet.label: CORRECT — InvokeAsync method injection
snippet.explanation: AppDbContext resolved from request scope each call. ASP.NET Core activates InvokeAsync parameters from RequestServices automatically.

snippet.label: IMiddleware with scoped service in constructor
snippet.explanation: IMiddlewareFactory creates middleware per request — scoped constructor injection is safe because the instance is not a singleton.

snippet.label: ValidateOnBuild catches captive dependencies at startup
snippet.explanation: Enable ValidateOnBuild in CI — captive middleware constructor injection fails at deploy time instead of under concurrent load in production.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Disabling ValidateScopes in production to silence startup errors. Storing resolved scoped service in middleware instance field during InvokeAsync for later requests. Resolving scoped service before request scope exists (background thread). Using BuildServiceProvider in middleware — creates orphan scope.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: concurrent integration tests hammering audit middleware — captive DbContext throws ObjectDisposedException or returns cross-request data. dotnet-counters track EF Core active DbContext count — should match in-flight requests, not grow unbounded. Application Insights exceptions mentioning 'second operation on same context'. Code review grep: middleware constructor parameters — flag any scoped-registered type. IMiddleware slightly increases per-request allocations — negligible vs correct semantics.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Scoped deps in ctor OK — instance per request
Captive dependency unless dependency is singleton
Singleton holding scoped in static field
Worst case — leaks across all requests

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Injecting DbContext in middleware constructor without acknowledging captive dependency. Saying 'DI handles it' without explaining singleton middleware lifetime. Not knowing IMiddleware or InvokeAsync injection exists. Unable to mention ValidateOnBuild / ValidateScopes.

interviewTakeaways: Convention-based middleware is singleton — never inject scoped services in constructor (captive dependency).
Resolve scoped deps via InvokeAsync parameters, IMiddleware, or HttpContext.RequestServices per request.
Production tip: ValidateOnBuild true in CI; load-test audit middleware; watch EF context count in counters.

60s: Middleware class is singleton at startup. Scoped DbContext in ctor is captive — one context forever, not thread-safe. Fix: InvokeAsync method injection or IMiddleware per request. ValidateOnBuild catches this at startup.
Follow-up: how does IHostedService get a scope for background work?
commonPitfalls: DbContext in middleware constructor gets you rejected — textbook captive dependency on the #1 middleware interview question.
Disabling ValidateScopes to ship — hides the bug until production concurrency.
Strong answer: 'Singleton middleware, scoped only in InvokeAsync or IMiddleware. ValidateOnBuild. EF context must not outlive request. Node compares to per-request pool connect vs module singleton.'
introducedIn: ASP.NET Core 1.0 DI; IMiddleware in 2.0; ValidateOnBuild in generic host

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node anti-pattern: const db = await connect() at module top level shared by all requests mirrors captive scoped injection. Correct pattern: attach client per request or use AsyncLocalStorage.
NestJS Scope.REQUEST providers are recreated per request like scoped services. Injecting REQUEST-scoped provider into singleton middleware fails validation — parallel to ASP.NET captive dependency.
